items.stem: Why is average accuracy alone a weak measure of agent reliability?

options.text: It can hide serious tail and failure-case behaviour that matters in production
options.rationale: Correct: a good average can mask rare but severe failures.
Averages are easy to compute; that is not the issue.
Averages are rarely perfect and this is not the point.
Accuracy is a quality measure; the concern is what it hides.

items.explanation: Correct: a good average can mask rare but severe failures.

items.stem: Which TWO belong in adversarial reliability testing? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Prompts crafted to make the agent misbehave or ignore instructions
options.rationale: Correct: adversarial prompts probe the agent's weak points.

options.text: Injecting tool and dependency failures to test recovery
options.rationale: Correct: failure injection checks how the agent handles broken dependencies.

options.text: Only testing inputs you already know succeed
options.rationale: Happy-path-only testing misses the failures that matter.
Without an evaluation set there is nothing to measure.

items.explanation: Correct: adversarial prompts probe the agent's weak points.

items.stem: A new agent version keeps the same average score but a key safety metric dropped. What should a reliability gate do?

options.text: Block the release because a tracked metric regressed
options.rationale: Correct: gates must act on per-metric regressions, not just the average.

options.text: Ship it because the average is unchanged
options.rationale: The average hides the regression the gate exists to catch.
Removing the metric hides the problem.
Turning off the gate defeats its purpose.

items.explanation: Correct: gates must act on per-metric regressions, not just the average.
